correct_answer: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses
question: Maya deposits $500 of her summer earnings at a bank. What does the bank usually do with much of the money while it sits in her account?
intro: A bank is a business that accepts deposits (money people put in accounts) and makes loans (money it lends and expects to be paid back with interest). Banks keep only part of their deposits as cash and lend much of the rest. The interest borrowers pay helps the bank pay its costs, earn a profit, and pay interest to savers.
feedback: Banks pool deposits and lend much of the money to borrowers. Maya can still withdraw her $500; the bank keeps enough cash and reserves on hand to meet withdrawals.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a bank stores each customer's own cash separately
misconceptions.C: Confuses a bank deposit with a tax payment
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank deposit with an investment account

correct_answer: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members
question: Which statement best describes a credit union?
intro: A credit union offers many of the same services as a bank: checking and savings accounts, debit cards, and loans. The difference is ownership. A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, who are its account holders. To join, you must meet its membership rules, such as living in an area, working for an employer, or belonging to a group.
feedback: Credit unions are member-owned, not-for-profit cooperatives. Profits are returned to members through lower fees, lower loan rates, or higher savings rates.

misconceptions.B: Thinks "credit" in the name means the government provides credit
misconceptions.C: Confuses a credit union with a brokerage firm
misconceptions.D: Describes a stock-owned bank, not a credit union

correct_answer: Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules
question: Jordan wants to join Riverside Teachers Credit Union, but Jordan is not a teacher and has no family member who works in a school. What is the most likely obstacle?
intro: Every credit union has a "field of membership": the group of people it is allowed to serve. It might be employees of certain companies, people who live or work in a county, or members of an organization. Family members of current members can often join too. Some credit unions let almost anyone join by first joining a partner organization.
feedback: A credit union can serve only people within its field of membership. Jordan should check its eligibility rules or look for a credit union whose field includes Jordan.

misconceptions.A: Thinks credit unions offer only loans
misconceptions.B: Confuses member ownership with buying publicly traded shares
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card is required to open an account

correct_answer: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts
question: A city has a large national bank, a local community bank, a credit union, and an online-only bank. Which feature is TRUE of all four kinds of institutions?
intro: Banks come in different types. National and regional banks are large and have many branches. Community banks are smaller and local. Online banks have no branches; customers use an app, a website, ATMs, and mobile deposit. Deposits at federally insured banks are protected by the FDIC, and deposits at federally insured credit unions by the NCUA, up to legal limits.
feedback: Federally insured banks (FDIC) and credit unions (NCUA) can all offer insured deposit accounts. Ownership, branches, and fees differ from one institution to another.

misconceptions.B: Credit union ownership applied to every institution
misconceptions.D: Confuses insured deposits with guaranteed investment returns

correct_answer: Losing the money to a fire or theft at home
question: Priya keeps $1,200 in cash in a shoebox. Which risk would a federally insured bank account reduce?
feedback: Insured deposits are protected from loss at home and from bank failure up to legal limits. An account does not stop prices from rising and does not decide how she spends.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a bank account removes the effect of inflation
misconceptions.B: Confuses where money is kept with taxes on purchases
misconceptions.C: Thinks an account controls spending habits by itself

correct_answer: A deposit
question: Aiden puts $40 into his savings account. What is this called?
intro: A deposit is money you put into an account. A withdrawal is money you take out. A loan is money a lender gives you that you must pay back, usually with interest.
feedback: Putting money into an account is a deposit. Taking money out is a withdrawal.

misconceptions.B: Thinks putting money in is borrowing
misconceptions.C: Confuses adding money with a charge

correct_answer: A withdrawal
question: Sofia takes $60 in cash out of her checking account at an ATM. What is this called?
intro: When you take money out of your own account, by cash at an ATM, a debit card purchase, or a check, it is a withdrawal. The money was already yours.
feedback: Taking your own money out of your account is a withdrawal; you do not owe it back.

misconceptions.D: Confuses money taken out with money earned

correct_answer: A loan
question: A bank gives Luis $8,000 to buy a used car, and Luis agrees to pay it back over four years with interest. What did Luis receive?
intro: A loan is borrowed money. The borrower promises to repay the amount borrowed, called the principal, plus interest, which is the price of borrowing.
feedback: Money that must be repaid with interest is a loan. Luis owes the $8,000 principal plus interest.

misconceptions.B: Thinks money received from a bank is a deposit
misconceptions.D: Confuses borrowed money with his own savings

correct_answer: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account
question: Which choice describes interest from a SAVER'S point of view?
intro: Interest works in two directions. A borrower pays interest to a lender for using the lender's money. A saver earns interest from a bank, because the bank uses the saver's deposits to make loans.
feedback: Savers earn interest; borrowers pay interest. The first amount deposited is the principal.

misconceptions.A: Confuses interest with a monthly fee

correct_answer: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers
question: Why can a bank afford to pay interest to savers?
feedback: A bank earns more interest from loans than it pays on deposits. The difference helps cover costs and profit.

misconceptions.C: Thinks interest is cancelled by a fee
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank with the central bank

correct_answer: Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank
question: A payment app advertises "bank-level" accounts. Its fine print says, "We are a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Harbor Bank, Member FDIC." What does this mean?
intro: Many apps that hold money are not banks. They are financial technology ("fintech") companies that partner with a bank. Money may be FDIC insured only if it is actually deposited at the partner bank in the customer's name and the records are kept properly. If the fintech company itself fails, getting access to money can take time.
feedback: The fine print says the deposits are at Harbor Bank. FDIC insurance protects against Harbor Bank failing, not against the app company failing.

misconceptions.A: Takes the advertising at face value
misconceptions.B: Ignores insurance through a partner bank
misconceptions.C: Misreads what a partner bank does

correct_answer: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?
question: Which question is MOST useful to ask before keeping a large balance in a payment app?
intro: Deposit insurance covers money in deposit accounts at insured banks. A balance kept in a payment app may not be a bank deposit at all, depending on how the app holds it. The app's terms explain where the money is held.
feedback: Whether the balance is a deposit at an insured bank, in your name, decides whether deposit insurance can apply.

misconceptions.D: Focuses on features rather than protection

correct_answer: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch
question: An online bank pays 4.0% on savings and charges no monthly fee, but it has no branches. A local bank pays 0.5% and has a branch near Ana's job. Ana is paid in cash tips each night. Which drawback of the online bank matters MOST for Ana?
intro: Online banks often pay higher savings rates and charge fewer fees because they have no branches to run. The trade-off is access: depositing cash can be hard or impossible, and help is by phone or chat. The best choice depends on how you use your money.
feedback: Ana deposits cash every night, so a way to deposit cash matters more to her than a higher rate. She might use both kinds of bank.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a higher savings rate is a drawback
misconceptions.B: Assumes online banks lack debit cards
misconceptions.C: Assumes no online bank is insured

correct_answer: Its deposits are insured up to the legal limit
question: A bank's website shows the FDIC logo. What does this tell a customer?
feedback: The FDIC sign means deposits are insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Investments sold at a bank are not deposits and are not FDIC insured.

misconceptions.A: Thinks FDIC insures a bank's stock

correct_answer: The app company fails and customers wait months to reach their money
question: Which situation shows the main risk of keeping money with a non-bank app?
feedback: When a fintech company fails, its records of who owns what must be sorted out before customers can get their money, even if a partner bank is insured.

misconceptions.B: Describes an advantage, not a risk

question: Two banks are similar except: Bank A charges a $12 monthly fee unless the balance stays above $1,500; Bank B charges no monthly fee. Kai usually keeps about $400 in checking. How much more would Bank A cost Kai per year?
intro: Fees add up. A monthly fee costs 12 times that amount in a year. Many banks waive a monthly fee if you meet a condition, such as a minimum balance or a direct deposit. If you will not meet the condition, plan to pay the fee.
feedback: Kai's $400 balance is below $1,500, so the fee applies every month: $12 × 12 = $144.

misconceptions.B: Uses one month instead of a year

correct_answer: How many fee-free ATMs are near home and school
question: Which comparison is MOST important for a student who will make frequent ATM withdrawals?
intro: When comparing institutions, start with how you will use the account: fees, ATM access, branch or app access, minimum balances, and the savings rate. A feature that matters to one person may not matter to another.
feedback: Frequent ATM users can pay fees each time they use an out-of-network ATM, so fee-free ATM access is the key comparison.

misconceptions.C: Compares a product the student will not use now

question: A credit union and a bank both offer free checking. The credit union pays 2.5% on savings; the bank pays 0.1%. On a $2,000 savings balance for one year (simple interest), how much more would the credit union pay?
intro: To compare savings rates, find the interest each account pays. For one year, interest ≈ balance × rate (with the rate written as a decimal). Then subtract.

misconceptions.D: Uses only the credit union's interest

correct_answer: The account's fee schedule
question: Which document lists every fee an account can charge, such as overdraft, wire, and paper statement fees?
feedback: Banks give a fee schedule (often part of the account agreement). Ads show the highlights; the fee schedule shows every charge.

misconceptions.C: Thinks a statement lists every possible fee
misconceptions.D: Thinks fees are printed on the card

correct_answer: Reading the fee conditions before choosing
question: Leo picks a bank only because it gave him a $200 bonus for opening an account. Six months later he notices $15 monthly fees. What step did he skip?
feedback: Six months of $15 fees is $90, and the fees continue every month. Bonuses often require conditions; the fee rules decide the long-run cost.

misconceptions.B: Treats the bonus as the main decision
misconceptions.C: Thinks the method of opening caused the fees
misconceptions.D: Thinks a credit card prevents account fees

correct_answer: Paying rent, bills, and everyday purchases
question: Tia's paycheck is deposited into her checking account. Which use is a checking account designed for?
intro: A checking account is a bank or credit union account for everyday money: receiving pay, paying bills, buying things with a debit card, and writing checks. Checking accounts usually pay little or no interest. Money you are setting aside for later usually goes in a savings account.
feedback: Checking accounts are transaction accounts for everyday spending and bills. Long-term savings and investments belong in other accounts.

misconceptions.B: Confuses checking with a brokerage account
misconceptions.C: Confuses an account with a loan

correct_answer: Directly from Noah's checking account
question: Noah buys groceries for $46.30 with his debit card. Where does the money come from?
intro: A debit card is linked to your checking account. When you pay with it, the money comes out of your account, usually within a day or two. A credit card is different: the card company lends you the money, and you pay it back later.
feedback: A debit card spends money already in the linked checking account. It is not a loan.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a debit card with a credit card
misconceptions.D: Thinks debit cards draw from savings

question: Ella's checking balance is $312.40. She pays a $95.25 phone bill and makes a $40.00 ATM withdrawal. What is her new balance?
intro: Your balance is the money in your account. Each withdrawal, debit card purchase, or bill payment is subtracted; each deposit is added. Keeping a running balance helps you avoid spending money you do not have.

misconceptions.D: Adds the payments instead of subtracting

correct_answer: Sam's available balance is $100 lower for a short time
question: At a gas pump, Sam's debit card is approved, and the bank places a $100 hold, even though Sam pumps only $38 of gas. What is the effect until the hold is released?
intro: Some merchants, such as gas stations, hotels, and car rentals, place a temporary "hold" on a debit card before they know the final amount. The hold lowers your AVAILABLE balance (what you can spend now) until the final charge posts and the extra is released, often within a few days.
feedback: The hold temporarily reduces the available balance by $100. When the $38 charge posts, the extra $62 is released.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a hold is the final charge
misconceptions.C: Thinks holds only apply to credit cards

correct_answer: The credit card
question: A thief steals Ava's wallet and uses both her debit card and her credit card. Which card generally gives her stronger legal protection against the thief's charges?
intro: Federal law limits what you owe when a card is used without permission. For credit cards, the most you can owe for unauthorized charges is $50. For debit cards, the limit depends on how quickly you report the loss: $50, $500, or more if you wait over 60 days after your statement. Debit card fraud also removes your own money until the bank investigates.
feedback: Federal law caps credit card liability for unauthorized charges at $50. Debit card liability depends on how quickly you report the loss: up to $50, up to $500, or more after 60 days. Meanwhile, a thief has spent your own money.

misconceptions.A: Assumes spending your own money gives more protection

correct_answer: A debit card
question: Which card spends money that is ALREADY in your bank account?
intro: "Debit" means taking money out of your account. A debit card takes money from your checking account. "Credit" means borrowing: a credit card company pays the store, and you owe the card company.
feedback: A debit card draws on money already in your checking account.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a credit card spends your own money
misconceptions.C: Confuses a prepaid gift card with a bank account card

correct_answer: The credit card company, and Owen owes it $25
question: Owen pays for a $25 meal with a credit card. Who pays the restaurant first?
intro: With a credit card, the card company pays the merchant for you. The amount is added to your card balance, which is a debt you must pay back. If you do not pay the full balance by the due date, you may owe interest.
feedback: The card company pays the restaurant; Owen now owes the card company $25.

misconceptions.D: Thinks the store waits to be paid

correct_answer: It is declined, or covered for an overdraft fee
question: What happens if you try to spend more with a debit card than your account holds?
intro: A debit card can only spend the money in your account. If a purchase is larger than your balance, the bank may decline it. If you opted in to overdraft coverage, the bank may pay it and charge an overdraft fee.
feedback: Spending past your balance leads to a declined purchase or an overdraft with a fee.

misconceptions.A: Thinks the bank absorbs the shortfall for free
misconceptions.B: Thinks the store adjusts the price
misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card always backs a debit card

correct_answer: Using a credit card creates a debt; using a debit card does not
question: Which statement is TRUE?
feedback: Credit cards are borrowing. Debit cards spend your own money.

correct_answer: A debit card with overdraft coverage turned off
question: Mia wants a card that will stop her from spending more than she has. Which card fits that goal better?
intro: If you do not opt in to overdraft coverage, a bank generally cannot charge you an overdraft fee for an ATM withdrawal or a one-time debit card purchase; instead the purchase is declined. A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit, which is not your money.
feedback: Without overdraft coverage, one-time debit card purchases above the balance are generally declined, so Mia cannot spend money she does not have.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a credit limit is her own money
misconceptions.B: Thinks purchase size changes how credit works

question: Rosa uses an out-of-network ATM. Her bank charges $2.50 and the ATM owner charges $3.00. She withdraws $40. How much leaves her account in total?
intro: An ATM network is a group of machines your bank lets you use without a fee. At an "out-of-network" ATM you can be charged twice: once by your own bank and once by the ATM's owner (a "surcharge").

misconceptions.C: Includes only the ATM owner's fee

question: Each out-of-network withdrawal costs Rosa $5.50 in fees: $2.50 from her bank and $3.00 from the ATM owner. She makes two such withdrawals a week. About how much does she pay in ATM fees in a year (52 weeks)?
intro: Small fees repeated often add up. Multiply the fee per use by the number of uses in a year.
feedback: Withdrawals per year: 2 × 52 = 104. Fees: $5.50 × 104 = $572.

misconceptions.A: Gives the fees for one withdrawal
misconceptions.D: Includes the $40 cash withdrawn each time

correct_answer: Use in-network ATMs or get cash back at stores
question: Rosa pays $5.50 in fees each time she withdraws cash at an out-of-network ATM. Which choice would cut her ATM fees the MOST?
feedback: In-network ATMs and cash back at stores usually have no fees. Smaller, more frequent withdrawals raise the total fees.

misconceptions.B: Smaller withdrawals mean more fees, not fewer
misconceptions.C: Thinks a different machine avoids fees

question: A bank refunds up to $10 of other banks' ATM fees each month. Rosa pays $22 in out-of-network fees this month. How much does she pay after the refund?
intro: Some accounts refund ATM fees up to a monthly limit. The refund lowers what you pay, but only up to that limit.

misconceptions.A: Gives the refund instead of what she pays

correct_answer: It can carry a fee even though no money is withdrawn
question: Which statement about an ATM "balance inquiry" at an out-of-network machine is MOST accurate?
feedback: Out-of-network ATMs may charge for balance checks. Checking the balance in your bank's app is usually free.

misconceptions.A: Assumes balance checks are free at any ATM
misconceptions.B: Confuses an inquiry with a transfer
misconceptions.C: Confuses an inquiry with a deposit

question: Kim's app shows: current balance $250; pending transactions −$80. What is her available balance?
intro: A transaction is "pending" when the bank knows about it but has not finished processing it ("posting" it). Your available balance is the money you can spend now: roughly your posted balance minus pending charges and holds. Spending based on the larger number can cause overdrafts.

correct_answer: Her available balance minus uncleared checks
question: Which balance should Kim use to decide whether she can afford a $150 purchase today?
intro: Bank apps show what the bank knows. A check you wrote that the payee has not cashed yet does not appear at all. Your own record of payments, called a register, catches those.
feedback: Her real spending power is the available balance minus payments the bank has not seen yet.

question: Ben deposits a $600 check on Monday. The bank says $225 is available Tuesday and the rest Thursday. How much can Ben safely spend from this deposit on Tuesday?
intro: When you deposit a check, the bank may "hold" part of the money until the check clears. Federal rules set the maximum hold times, and the bank must tell you when the money will be available.
feedback: Only $225 is available Tuesday; the remaining $375 becomes available Thursday.

misconceptions.D: Assumes the whole deposit is available at once
misconceptions.C: Gives the amount held until Thursday
misconceptions.A: Thinks none of a check is available early

correct_answer: The bank takes the amount back from your account, possibly with a fee
question: If a deposited check "bounces" (is returned unpaid) after you spent the money, what usually happens?
feedback: A returned check is reversed out of your account. If you already spent the money, your balance can go negative, and fees may apply. This is how fake-check scams harm victims.

misconceptions.C: Assumes fees are always passed on
misconceptions.D: Thinks a posted deposit cannot be reversed

correct_answer: Recording each purchase as you make it
question: Which habit best prevents spending based on the wrong balance?
feedback: Recording each transaction as it happens keeps your own balance current, including items the bank has not seen yet.

misconceptions.C: Ignores pending items and uncleared checks

correct_answer: Open a joint teen account with a parent or guardian
question: Jordan is 17 and wants a first checking account. Which plan matches how most banks handle an applicant under 18?
intro: Banks and credit unions usually require an adult (18 or older) to open an account alone, because a minor generally cannot be held to a contract. Many offer teen or student checking accounts that a minor opens jointly with a parent or guardian. The adult co-owner can see the account and shares responsibility for it.
feedback: Most institutions let a minor open a checking account only as a joint or teen account with an adult co-owner.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a school ID meets the identity requirements
misconceptions.B: Invents a minimum age for every account
misconceptions.C: Thinks sharing someone else's account is safe or allowed

correct_answer: Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN
question: Which information will a bank most likely require to open a checking account?
intro: Federal rules require banks to verify who opens an account. Before opening one, a bank collects at least your name, date of birth, address, and an identification number: a Social Security number for U.S. citizens, or another number, such as an ITIN or passport number, for others. Most banks also ask for a government-issued photo ID.
feedback: The Customer Identification Program rule requires name, date of birth, address, and an ID number; banks usually also check a photo ID.

misconceptions.B: Thinks sharing a PIN is part of opening an account

correct_answer: Account X: $0; Account Y: $60
question:
Tess will receive about $800 a month by direct deposit and usually keeps about $300 in checking.
Account X: $10 monthly fee, waived with a direct deposit of $500 or more each month.
Account Y: $5 monthly fee, waived if the balance stays at $1,000 or more.
What would each account cost Tess in monthly fees over a year?
intro: Many checking accounts charge a monthly maintenance fee that is waived if you meet a condition: a minimum balance, a minimum direct deposit, or being a student. Compare accounts by the fees YOU would actually pay, based on how you will use the account.
feedback: Tess's $800 direct deposit meets Account X's $500 condition, so X costs $0. Her $300 balance is below Y's $1,000, so Y costs $5 × 12 = $60.

misconceptions.B: Ignores Account X's direct deposit waiver
misconceptions.C: Assumes Tess meets Account Y's $1,000 balance rule

correct_answer: Her bank's routing number and her account number
question: Tess wants her paycheck deposited directly into her new account. What does her employer need from her?
intro: Direct deposit sends pay electronically into your account. Your employer needs two numbers: the routing number, a 9-digit number that identifies your bank, and your account number, which identifies your account at that bank. Both appear on checks and in the bank's app. Never share a PIN or password to set up a deposit.
feedback: Routing number plus account number tells the payroll system exactly where to send the money. PINs and passwords are never needed.

misconceptions.A: Confuses a debit card with the account itself; unsafe
misconceptions.B: Thinks an employer needs login credentials; unsafe
misconceptions.C: Thinks a bank name identifies a specific account

question: Ahmed's new account requires a $25 opening deposit and has a $6 monthly fee that is waived only when the balance stays at $300 or more. Ahmed's balance stays around $150. Assuming no other fees, how much will the account charge him in fees over 6 months?
feedback: The fee applies every month because $150 is below $300: $6 × 6 = $36. The $25 opening deposit is Ahmed's own money in the account, not a fee.

misconceptions.D: Adds the opening deposit as if it were a fee

correct_answer: The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies
question: A checking account has a "$12 monthly maintenance fee." What does this mean?
intro: A fee is a charge the bank takes from your account. A "monthly maintenance fee" (also called a service fee) is charged every month just for having the account, unless you meet a waiver condition.
feedback: A monthly maintenance fee is taken from your account each month unless you qualify for a waiver.

misconceptions.C: Confuses a fee with a deposit requirement
misconceptions.D: Thinks a monthly fee is charged once

question: An account waives its $8 monthly fee "with a minimum daily balance of $500." In March, Lena's balance stays above $600 every day. What fee does she pay for March?
intro: A waiver condition is a rule that, if you meet it, cancels a fee. A "minimum daily balance" rule means your balance must stay at or above the amount every day of the statement period.
feedback: Lena's balance never dropped below $500, so the fee is waived: $0.

misconceptions.D: Confuses the balance requirement with a fee

question: An account waives its $8 monthly fee "with a minimum daily balance of $500." In April, Lena's balance drops to $450 for one day, then goes back above $600. What fee does she pay for April?
intro: With a minimum daily balance rule, one day below the minimum is enough to lose the waiver for that month, even if the balance is high on other days.
feedback: One day at $450 is below $500, so the $8 fee applies for April.

misconceptions.A: Uses the average or ending balance instead of the daily minimum

correct_answer: It is your own money, deposited into your new account
question: Which statement about a minimum opening deposit is TRUE?
feedback: An opening deposit is the first money you put into the account. It stays yours.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a deposit with a fee
misconceptions.C: Confuses a deposit with a loan
misconceptions.D: Confuses an opening deposit with a monthly fee

correct_answer: One whose fee is waived for students, if the student qualifies
question: Two accounts are identical except for fees. Which would cost a student nothing?
feedback: Only an account whose fee the student can actually avoid costs nothing.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a small fee is the same as no fee
misconceptions.B: Ignores whether the student can meet the waiver
misconceptions.C: Overlooks that $6 every other month still adds up

question: A disclosure says: "Paper statement fee: $2 per month. Free with e-statements." Rafael wants paper statements. Over two years, how much will this choice cost?
intro: When you open an account, the bank gives you disclosures: documents that list the account's interest rate, fees, and rules. Federal law (the Truth in Savings Act) requires banks to disclose this information. Small optional fees, like paper statement fees, are easy to miss.
feedback: $2 per month × 24 months = $48.

correct_answer: The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer
question: Which item would you expect to find in an account's fee schedule?
intro: A fee schedule is a list of every fee the account can charge: monthly fees, overdraft and returned item fees, wire transfer fees, stop payment fees, out-of-network ATM fees, and fees for extras like paper statements or cashier's checks.
feedback: Wire transfer fees are account fees listed in a fee schedule.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fee schedule with a loan rate sheet
misconceptions.D: Confuses a deposit fee schedule with a card agreement

correct_answer: The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used
question: An account advertises "No monthly fee!" Its fee schedule lists a $35 overdraft fee, a $3 out-of-network ATM fee, and a $30 wire fee. Which conclusion is correct?
feedback: "No monthly fee" covers only the maintenance fee. Other fees apply when you use certain services or overdraw.

misconceptions.A: Treats the ad as the whole story
misconceptions.B: Adds possible fees as if all are charged monthly
misconceptions.C: Thinks a free account cannot have any fees

correct_answer: Compare the new terms with other accounts
question: A bank sends a notice that a fee will change in 30 days. What is a reasonable response?
intro: Banks can change account terms. They must tell existing customers in advance about changes that could hurt them, such as a higher fee. That notice gives you time to compare and decide.
feedback: Advance notice lets you compare and, if needed, move your money before the change takes effect.

misconceptions.B: Thinks account terms are fixed forever
misconceptions.D: Invents a way to lock in fees

correct_answer: Which fees will I realistically pay, given how I bank?
question: Which question is MOST useful when comparing two accounts' disclosures?
feedback: Your real cost depends on your habits: balance, deposits, ATM use, and overdraft risk.

misconceptions.A: Uses size as a measure of cost
misconceptions.B: Uses document length as a measure of cost
misconceptions.C: Uses advertising as a measure of cost

correct_answer: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
question: Devon's application for a checking account is denied because of a report from a checking account screening company. What kind of history does such a report usually show?
intro: Before opening an account, many banks check a consumer report from a checking account screening company, such as ChexSystems or Early Warning Services. These reports list problems with past accounts, such as unpaid overdrafts, accounts closed by a bank, or suspected fraud. Negative information can stay on these reports for years.
feedback: Screening reports focus on past deposit-account problems, such as unpaid negative balances or fraud.

correct_answer: Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error
question: Devon was denied a checking account because of a checking account screening report that he believes contains a mistake. What can he do?
intro: Checking account screening companies are consumer reporting agencies. Under federal law you can get a free copy of your report every 12 months and dispute information you believe is wrong; the company must investigate.
feedback: Like credit reports, screening reports can be requested for free each year and disputed when wrong.

correct_answer: Pay off the $90 and ask the old bank to update the report
question: Devon's checking account screening report correctly shows a $90 negative balance he left at an old bank. Which step would most likely help him open an account in the future?
feedback: Paying what is owed and having the record updated to "paid" improves his chances. Keeping cash at home adds theft and loss risks.

misconceptions.D: Gives up the protection of an insured account

correct_answer: An account for people with past account problems, often with limits
question: What is a "second-chance" checking account?
intro: Some banks and credit unions offer second-chance accounts to people who were denied regular accounts. They may have a monthly fee, no overdraft feature, or lower limits. After a period of good use, some can be changed to a regular account.
feedback: Second-chance accounts help people rebuild banking history, often with limits or fees.

misconceptions.B: Confuses an account with a loan

correct_answer: Check-cashing fees on every paycheck can cost far more over a year
question: Devon cannot open a regular account, but a credit union offers him a second-chance checking account (an account for people with past account problems, often with a small fee). Why might it be better than using check-cashing stores for every paycheck?
feedback: For example, 2% of a $900 paycheck every two weeks is $18 per check, about $468 a year, which is usually much more than an account's fees.

misconceptions.A: Assumes check cashing has no fees
misconceptions.C: Thinks an account prevents all overdrafts

question: Nina starts with $215.60 in checking. She deposits $84.25, buys shoes for $59.99, and pays a $42.00 bill. What is her balance?
intro: An account register (or a budgeting app) records every transaction and keeps a running balance. Add each deposit (money in). Subtract each withdrawal, payment, or purchase (money out). Recording each item as it happens shows what you truly have.

misconceptions.D: Adds the purchases instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit instead of adding

question: A bank statement shows: beginning balance $640.00; total deposits $1,120.00; total withdrawals $1,395.50. What is the ending balance?
intro: A bank statement summarizes one period, usually a month: the balance at the start, every deposit and withdrawal, any fees or interest, and the balance at the end. Ending balance = beginning balance + deposits − withdrawals.

misconceptions.D: Adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts withdrawals from deposits but leaves out the beginning balance
misconceptions.C: Adds the beginning balance to withdrawals and subtracts deposits

question: A statement shows a beginning balance of $410.00, withdrawals of $760.00, and an ending balance of $300.00. What were the total deposits?
intro: The statement equation (beginning + deposits − withdrawals = ending) can be used to find any missing amount. Substitute what you know and solve for the unknown.

misconceptions.B: Subtracts instead of solving for the missing amount

question: Carlos's balance is $42.10. A $55.00 automatic payment goes through anyway. What does his account show afterward?
intro: If more money leaves an account than it holds, the balance becomes negative: the account is "overdrawn." A negative balance is money owed to the bank, often with a fee added. It must be repaid by depositing money.
feedback: $42.10 − $55.00 = −$12.90. Carlos owes the bank $12.90, plus any overdraft fee.

misconceptions.C: Ignores the sign; thinks the account still has money
misconceptions.B: Thinks a balance cannot go below zero

correct_answer: The landlord had not yet deposited the check when the statement closed
question: Ivy wrote a $75 check to her landlord on May 30. Her May 31 bank statement does not show it. Why?
intro: A check you write is paid only when the person you paid deposits or cashes it, which can take days or weeks. Until then, the money is still in your account, but it is already promised.
feedback: An "outstanding" check has been written but not yet cashed. It will appear later, so Ivy's register must still subtract it.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a missing item means the payment is cancelled

correct_answer: A paycheck deposited by direct deposit
question: Which transaction INCREASES a checking account balance?
intro: Money coming into an account (deposits, direct deposits, transfers in, interest) is a credit and increases the balance. Money going out (purchases, withdrawals, bill payments, fees) is a debit and decreases it.
feedback: A deposit is money in; the other three are money out.

correct_answer: A $3.00 ATM fee
question: On a bank statement, which item is a debit?
intro: On a bank statement, "debit" means money taken out of the account, and "credit" means money added. Fees are debits; interest earned and refunds are credits.
feedback: The fee is taken from the account, so it is a debit.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a transfer in is money out
misconceptions.C: Thinks a refund is money out

correct_answer: It goes down to $90
question: Zoe's balance is $120. She buys a $30 jacket. What happens to her balance?
intro: Each purchase with a debit card lowers your balance by the purchase amount.

misconceptions.C: Thinks purchases wait until month end
misconceptions.D: Confuses the price with the new balance

correct_answer: So your balance shows what you really have left to spend
question: Why should you record a purchase in your register right away?
feedback: Recording each item immediately keeps your running balance accurate.

misconceptions.B: Thinks unrecorded items are not charged

correct_answer: A check you wrote, a bill payment, and a monthly fee
question: Which list contains ONLY items that lower a balance?
feedback: Checks you write, bill payments, and fees are all money out.

misconceptions.D: Lists only items that add money

question: Sam's statement ending balance is $520. He has a $150 deposit the bank had not received yet and two outstanding checks of $60 and $45. What is his adjusted (true) balance?
intro: Reconciling means checking that your records match the bank's. Start with the statement's ending balance, add deposits the bank has not recorded yet ("deposits in transit"), and subtract checks and payments that have not cleared ("outstanding"). The result should equal your register balance.

misconceptions.B: Uses the statement balance without adjusting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit and the checks

correct_answer: A $10 charge on the statement was never recorded in his register
question: Sam reconciles his account. After he adds deposits in transit and subtracts outstanding checks, the statement shows $565, but his register shows $575. Which is the most likely explanation?
intro: When the adjusted statement balance and the register do not match, look for items on the statement that are missing from the register, such as fees, interest, or automatic payments, and for math mistakes in the register.
feedback: A $10 fee or charge that Sam did not record would make his register $10 too high.

misconceptions.B: Would make the adjusted balance lower, not his register higher

correct_answer: Subtract $4 from his register balance
question: Sam finds a $4 monthly "service fee" on his statement that he did not record. What should he do in his register?
feedback: A fee is money out, so Sam subtracts $4 to keep his register correct.

misconceptions.C: Thinks only one record needs updating

correct_answer: It catches errors and unauthorized charges early
question: Which reason BEST explains why reconciling monthly matters?
feedback: Spotting problems early matters because reporting deadlines apply to unauthorized transfers and errors.

question: Amy's statement ending balance is $310. Outstanding checks: $25 and $40. No deposits in transit. Her register shows $245. Do her records agree?
feedback: $310 − $65 = $245, which matches her register.

correct_answer: Contact his bank right away to report the unauthorized charge
question: Lucas sees a $129 charge from an online store he has never used. What should he do FIRST?
intro: An unauthorized transaction is one you did not make or allow. Federal rules (Regulation E) limit your liability for unauthorized electronic transfers, but the protection depends on how fast you report. Contact your bank as soon as you notice one.
feedback: Reporting quickly keeps his liability limits as low as possible.

misconceptions.B: Shares sensitive data with an unknown party

correct_answer: Yes; it is within 60 days of the statement
question: Mia's statement dated March 31 shows an unauthorized online debit charge; her card was never lost or stolen. She reports it on May 20. Is she within the window for full protection?
intro: For unauthorized electronic transfers that appear on a statement, you generally have 60 days after the statement is sent to report them. After that, you may be liable for later transfers the bank could have stopped.
feedback: March 31 to May 20 is 50 days, inside the 60-day window. If a card is lost or stolen, report within 2 business days of learning of it for the lowest limit ($50).

correct_answer: This is an error she can dispute with the bank or the store
question: A store charged Ana twice for one $45 purchase. Which statement is accurate?
feedback: A duplicate charge is an error. She can ask the store for a refund and dispute it with her bank.

misconceptions.B: Thinks using the card waives rights
misconceptions.C: Thinks closing the account is the only fix

correct_answer: Transaction alerts and frequent app checks
question: Which habit catches unauthorized charges the fastest?
feedback: Alerts and frequent checks spot problems within days.

question: Ben lost his debit card on Monday, noticed it Tuesday, and reported it Tuesday. A thief spent $300 before he reported it. What is the most Ben can be held responsible for under federal rules?
intro: For a lost or stolen debit card, if you report within 2 business days of learning of the loss, your liability for unauthorized transfers is capped at $50. After 2 business days, the cap rises to $500. Many banks voluntarily offer $0 liability, but the law sets these limits.
feedback: He reported within 2 business days of learning of the loss, so the legal cap is $50.

misconceptions.A: Thinks he owes everything the thief spent
misconceptions.B: Uses the limit for late reports
misconceptions.C: Assumes there is never any liability

correct_answer: Spending more than the account holds
question: What is an overdraft?
intro: An overdraft happens when a payment or purchase is larger than the money in the account and the bank pays it anyway. The account goes negative, and the bank may charge an overdraft fee. If the bank refuses the payment instead, the item is returned unpaid, and a returned-item ("NSF") fee may apply.
feedback: An overdraft means the account was overdrawn: the balance went below zero.

misconceptions.A: Confuses an overdraft with an installment loan
misconceptions.C: Confuses an overdraft with a transfer

question: Mason's balance is $30. His bank charges $35 per overdraft. He makes three debit card purchases: $12, then $25, then $8, and he has opted in to overdraft coverage. If each purchase that makes the balance negative (or more negative) gets a fee, how much will he pay in fees?
intro: Each item paid while the account is overdrawn can trigger its own fee. Track the balance item by item. A small purchase can cost far more than its price once a fee is added.

misconceptions.D: Charges a fee on every purchase
misconceptions.A: Uses the amount overdrawn as the fee

correct_answer: The purchase is declined, with no overdraft fee
question: Without opting in to overdraft coverage, what usually happens when Leah tries a one-time debit card purchase larger than her balance?
intro: Federal rules say a bank must get your permission (your "opt-in") before charging overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases. If you do not opt in, those transactions are usually declined. Checks and automatic bill payments are treated differently and can still be overdrawn.
feedback: Without opt-in, one-time debit purchases above the balance are usually declined, so no overdraft fee applies.

misconceptions.C: Thinks the store absorbs the shortfall

question: Hana links her savings account to checking for overdraft protection. The bank charges $10 per automatic transfer instead of a $35 overdraft fee. She overdraws twice this month. How much does linking save her this month?
intro: Overdraft protection links checking to another account, such as savings or a line of credit. When checking runs short, money is moved automatically to cover the item. Banks often charge a transfer fee, but it is usually smaller than an overdraft fee.
feedback: Without linking: 2 × $35 = $70. With linking: 2 × $10 = $20. Savings: $70 − $20 = $50.

misconceptions.A: Gives the transfer fees instead of the savings

correct_answer: He may owe a returned-item fee, and the bill is still unpaid
question: Ray's $80 electric bill payment is returned unpaid because his account is short. Which result is MOST likely?
feedback: A returned (NSF) payment can cost a bank fee and a late fee from the biller, and the bill remains due.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a returned payment still counts
misconceptions.C: Thinks a failed payment erases the debt
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank pays at no cost

question: Rina's balance is $20. She spends $26. If the bank pays it, what is her balance (before any fee)?
intro: When spending is larger than the balance and the bank pays anyway, the balance becomes negative. A negative balance means you owe the bank that amount.

misconceptions.B: Thinks the bank stops at zero

correct_answer: Rina owes the bank $6
question: What does a balance of −$6 mean?
intro: A negative account balance is a debt to the bank. You must deposit enough to bring the balance back to zero or above.
feedback: A negative balance is money owed to the bank.

misconceptions.C: Thinks a negative balance closes the account

question: Rina's balance is −$6, and the bank adds a $35 overdraft fee. What is her new balance?
intro: A fee is subtracted from the balance, even when the balance is already negative, which makes it more negative.

misconceptions.D: Adds the fee to a positive 6
misconceptions.C: Subtracts 6 from 35 and keeps the sign

question: How much must Rina deposit to bring a −$41 balance back to exactly $0?
feedback: She must deposit $41 to cover both the shortfall and the fee.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a negative balance resets itself

correct_answer: Checking her available balance before the $26 purchase
question: Rina had $20 in checking and made a $26 debit purchase, overdrawing her account. Which choice would have prevented this?
feedback: Knowing the available balance before buying prevents overdrafts.

misconceptions.C: Checks too late to prevent the overdraft

question: Jae overdraws about once a month and pays a $34 fee each time. How much does that cost him in a year?
intro: A habit that causes a fee every month becomes a large yearly cost. Multiply the monthly cost by 12 to see the yearly impact.

correct_answer: Each small purchase really cost over $40
question: Jae pays a $34 overdraft fee about once a month, usually on debit purchases of under $10. What does that suggest about the true cost of those purchases?
feedback: A $9 purchase plus a $34 fee costs $43, almost five times the price.

correct_answer: Set a low-balance alert and keep a small buffer in checking
question: Jae overdraws about once a month because he buys things without checking his balance. Which step would MOST directly prevent his overdrafts?
intro: Low-balance alerts warn you before you overspend. A buffer, a small amount you treat as untouchable, absorbs timing surprises such as a bill that posts a day early.
feedback: Alerts plus a buffer address the cause: spending without knowing the balance.

misconceptions.A: The account is still the same
misconceptions.C: Statements arrive too late to prevent them

correct_answer: The buffer saves $408 and stays his money
question: Jae pays $408 a year in overdraft fees (12 × $34). Keeping a $100 buffer, money he leaves in checking and never spends, would have prevented all 12 overdrafts. Compare keeping the buffer with paying the fees.
feedback: The buffer remains in his account, while fees are gone forever.

misconceptions.C: Treats money kept as money lost

correct_answer: Read the current fee schedule or ask the bank directly
question: Some banks have reduced or ended overdraft fees, and others still charge them. What is the best way to learn your own bank's current policy?
feedback: Overdraft policies differ by bank and change over time; the current fee schedule is the authority.

question: An overdraft line of credit covers shortfalls with a loan that charges 18% APR. Kim borrows $200 through it and repays it after one month. About how much interest does she pay (simple interest for 1/12 of a year)?
intro: An overdraft line of credit is a small loan account linked to checking. When checking runs short, it lends the difference, and you pay interest (and sometimes a fee) until you repay it. Interest for part of a year ≈ principal × annual rate × fraction of a year.

correct_answer: The line of credit, by $27
question: Kim compares two ways to cover a $200 shortfall for one month: a $35 overdraft fee, or about $3 of interest plus a $5 transfer fee on her line of credit. Which costs less and by how much?
feedback: Line of credit: $3 + $5 = $8. Overdraft: $35. Difference: $27.

correct_answer: Unpaid amounts keep collecting interest
question: Which risk applies to an overdraft line of credit but NOT to a savings-linked transfer?
feedback: A line of credit is a loan; a savings link moves your own money.

correct_answer: Your credit history, because it is a loan
question: Which account would a bank usually check before approving an overdraft line of credit?
feedback: Because a line of credit is lending, the bank reviews your creditworthiness.

misconceptions.C: Confuses deposit terms with credit approval

question: Kim leaves $200 unpaid on the 18% line of credit for a full year (simple interest). How much interest accrues?

misconceptions.D: Gives the total owed instead of the interest

correct_answer: Savings usually earns more and stays apart from spending money
question: Why do people usually keep money for a goal six months away in a savings account rather than in checking?
intro: A savings account is a deposit account for money you are setting aside. It usually pays more interest than checking, and keeping savings separate makes it less likely you will spend it by accident. You can generally withdraw when you need to, though some banks limit how often.
feedback: Savings earns more and keeps goal money apart from spending money. Both checking and savings are deposits that can be insured.

misconceptions.B: Confuses savings with a certificate of deposit
misconceptions.D: Confuses saving with a guaranteed high return

question: A savings account pays 3.5% interest per year. About how much interest will $1,600 earn in one year?
intro: Interest for one year ≈ balance × annual rate (as a decimal). To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100: 3.5% = 0.035.

misconceptions.D: Gives the new balance instead of the interest

question: Grace has $300,000 in one individual savings account at a single FDIC-insured bank. If the bank failed, how much of her deposit would be above the standard insurance limit?
intro: The FDIC insures deposits at insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category (such as individual or joint). Credit union deposits have the same coverage through the NCUA. No depositor has lost insured funds since the FDIC began in 1934.
feedback: $300,000 − $250,000 = $50,000 is above the standard limit for one owner at one bank in one category.

misconceptions.A: Thinks every dollar is always insured
misconceptions.C: Confuses the insured part with the uninsured part

correct_answer: No: investments are not deposits, even when sold at a bank
question: Leo buys shares of a stock mutual fund through an investment desk inside his bank's branch. The fund loses value. Does FDIC insurance cover the loss?
intro: FDIC insurance covers deposits: checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, and certificates of deposit. It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, crypto assets, annuities, or life insurance, even if a bank sells them. It also does not protect against investment losses.
feedback: Mutual funds are investments, not deposits, so FDIC insurance does not cover their losses.

misconceptions.B: Applies the deposit limit to market losses
misconceptions.C: Thinks the source of money changes coverage

correct_answer: An insured savings account
question: Ava needs money she can reach quickly for unexpected costs and does not want it to lose value. Which place fits best?
feedback: An insured savings account keeps money safe, available, and earning some interest.

misconceptions.A: Chooses past performance over safety and access
misconceptions.C: Ignores theft, loss, and lost interest

correct_answer: Money set aside for a laptop you plan to buy next spring
question: Which money belongs in savings rather than checking?
intro: Checking is for money you will spend soon: bills and everyday purchases. Savings is for money you are setting aside for later: goals and emergencies.
feedback: Money for a later goal belongs in savings.

correct_answer: The bank adds money to her account
question: Leila earns 2% interest on her $500 savings for a year. What does "earning interest" mean here?
intro: Interest on savings is money the bank pays you for keeping your money there. It is added to your balance.
feedback: 2% of $500 is $10, which the bank adds to her account.

misconceptions.B: Confuses interest earned with a fee

question: What is 2% written as a decimal?
intro: Percent means "per hundred." To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100 (move the decimal point two places left).

question: Using 0.02 for 2%, how much interest does $500 earn in one year?

correct_answer: Its value in dollars does not go down because of market changes
question: Which statement is TRUE about money in an insured savings account?
feedback: Insured deposits do not lose dollars to market swings, though inflation can still reduce what the money buys.

correct_answer: The APY of each account
question:
Two savings accounts show:
Bank A: interest rate 4.00%, compounded monthly; APY 4.07%
Bank B: APY 4.05%
Which number should Mo use to compare them fairly?
intro: The interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding. APY (annual percentage yield) shows what you actually earn in a year once interest is added to your balance and itself earns interest (compounding). Banks must show APY for savings, so use APY to compare accounts.
feedback: APY includes compounding, so comparing APY to APY is fair. Bank A (4.07%) earns slightly more than Bank B (4.05%).

question: An account has an APY of 4.07%. About how much will $2,000 earn in one year if the rate stays the same and nothing is withdrawn?
intro: APY is the actual percent your money grows in one year, so one year of earnings ≈ balance × APY.

misconceptions.D: Gives the balance, not the interest

correct_answer: Interest that is added during the year also earns interest
question: Why is APY usually a little higher than the stated interest rate?
intro: APY (annual percentage yield) is the percent your money actually grows in one year. The stated interest rate is the yearly rate before compounding.
feedback: With compounding, earlier interest earns interest too, so the yearly yield is above the stated rate.

correct_answer: The bank can change the rate over time
question: A savings rate is "variable." What does that mean?
intro: Most savings accounts have variable rates: the bank can raise or lower them, often when market interest rates change. A certificate of deposit usually locks a rate for its term.
feedback: Variable means the bank may change it; past or advertised rates are not promises.

question: An ad shows "5.00% APY*", and the fine print says "*on balances up to $1,000; 0.50% APY on the amount above $1,000." Sara deposits $5,000. About how much interest will she earn in one year?
Marcus has $200,000 in an individual account at Bank A and $200,000 in an individual account at Bank B. Both banks are FDIC insured and separate. How much of his money is insured?
intro: The $250,000 limit applies per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Money at two different banks is insured separately. (Two "brands" of the same bank are one bank for insurance purposes.)
feedback: Each bank insures his $200,000 individually: $400,000 total.

misconceptions.C: Applies one limit across different banks
misconceptions.A: Thinks large balances are never insured

question: Sam and Pat own a joint account with $500,000 at one insured bank. Joint accounts are insured up to $250,000 per co-owner. How much is insured?
intro: Joint accounts are a separate ownership category from individual accounts. Each co-owner's share of joint accounts at one bank is insured up to $250,000.
feedback: Two co-owners × $250,000 = $500,000 of coverage, which covers the whole balance.

misconceptions.B: Applies one limit to the whole joint account

correct_answer: A 12-month certificate of deposit
question: Which product is covered by FDIC insurance when bought at an insured bank?
feedback: CDs are deposits. Investments, crypto assets, and safe deposit box contents are not insured deposits.

misconceptions.A: Thinks funds sold at banks are insured
misconceptions.B: Thinks crypto at a bank is insured

correct_answer: That claim does not mean the funds are FDIC insured
question: A website for a company that sells crypto says, "Your funds are safe — like a bank." What should a careful saver conclude?
intro: Only deposits at FDIC-insured banks (or NCUA-insured credit unions) are covered by deposit insurance. The FDIC warns consumers about companies that misrepresent their products as FDIC insured.
feedback: Comparisons to banks are not insurance. Check the FDIC's BankFind tool to see if an institution is an insured bank, and remember crypto assets are not deposits.

misconceptions.A: Treats a comparison as a guarantee

correct_answer: Move $10,000 or more to an account at a different insured bank
question: Ella has $260,000 in one individual account at an insured bank and wants all of it insured. Which change would accomplish that most directly?
feedback: Coverage is per bank per category. Two individual accounts at the same bank share one $250,000 limit; a second bank adds coverage.

misconceptions.B: Thinks multiple accounts in one category add coverage

correct_answer: One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars
question: Nora writes a check for $1,254.07. How should she write the amount in words on the check?
intro: A check is a written order telling your bank to pay someone from your account. You write the date, the payee (who gets paid), the amount in numbers, the amount in words with cents as a fraction of 100, and your signature. The words are the legal amount if the two differ.
feedback: $1,254.07 is written "One thousand two hundred fifty-four and 07/100 dollars."

misconceptions.C: Uses "point" instead of the cents fraction

correct_answer: His signature and "For deposit only"
question: Ben receives a paycheck made out to him and wants to deposit it at an ATM. What should he write on the back?
intro: To deposit or cash a check made out to you, you "endorse" it by signing the back. Adding "For deposit only" (a restrictive endorsement) means the check can only be deposited, which protects it if it is lost. For mobile deposit, banks often require "For mobile deposit only" too.
feedback: Signing with "For deposit only" endorses the check and limits it to being deposited.

misconceptions.B: Writes sensitive data on a check
misconceptions.C: Thinks the balance goes on the check

correct_answer: Payments she authorized are often hard or impossible to reverse
question: Mia sends $60 through a payment app to someone selling concert tickets online. The tickets never arrive. Which statement is most accurate?
intro: Peer-to-peer (P2P) payment apps move money quickly between people. Money you send yourself, even to a scammer, is usually treated as authorized and is often hard to get back. Federal error protections focus on transfers you did not authorize. Use P2P apps mainly with people you know and trust.
feedback: Because Mia authorized the payment, getting it back depends on the app's or bank's voluntary policies. Protections are stronger for unauthorized transfers.

misconceptions.C: Thinks the law forces a scammer to deliver

correct_answer: Keep it until the deposit is final, then destroy it
question: After depositing a check with his phone, what should Kai do with the paper check?
intro: Mobile check deposit lets you photograph a signed check in your bank's app. The bank may hold part of the money for a few days. Keep the paper check until the deposit is final, then destroy it securely so it cannot be deposited twice or misused.
feedback: Keep it until the funds are final in case the bank needs it, then shred it.

misconceptions.C: Discards it before the deposit is confirmed

correct_answer: A check or an electronic transfer from her bank account
question: Zara's landlord asks for rent in a way that leaves a record of payment. Which method fits BEST?
feedback: Checks and bank transfers leave records Zara can use as proof of payment.

correct_answer: An online bill payment or automatic transfer
question: Which payment method moves money directly from your bank account electronically on a date you set?
intro: Common ways to pay: cash; debit cards and checks (from your account); electronic transfers such as online bill pay and automatic payments (from your account, electronically); credit cards (borrowed money); and prepaid or gift cards (money loaded in advance).
feedback: Online bill pay and automatic payments take money from your account electronically.

misconceptions.B: Confuses borrowing with paying from your account
misconceptions.C: Confuses prepaid value with an account payment

correct_answer: Cash with no receipt
question: Which method gives the LEAST proof that you paid?
intro: A payment record proves you paid. Bank statements, cleared checks, and confirmation numbers are records. Cash leaves no record unless you get a receipt.
feedback: Cash without a receipt leaves no proof of payment.

misconceptions.A: A cleared check is a record

question: A gift card loaded with $50 is used to buy a $12 item. What is left on the card?
intro: A prepaid or gift card holds a set amount of money. Each purchase is subtracted until the card reaches $0.

misconceptions.C: Thinks the card balance does not change
misconceptions.A: Confuses the price with what is left

correct_answer: The person or business that receives the money
question: Who is the "payee" on a check?
feedback: The payee is named on the "Pay to the order of" line.

misconceptions.B: Confuses payee with the account holder

correct_answer: Paying a stranger online before receiving the item
question: Which situation makes a payment app MOST risky to use?
feedback: Paying strangers in advance is how many P2P scams work, because payments are hard to reverse.

correct_answer: A wire transfer
question: Which payment is generally the hardest to reverse once sent?
intro: A wire transfer moves money between banks quickly, often the same day, and is generally final once sent. ACH transfers (used for direct deposit and online bill pay) move money between bank accounts more slowly and have some ways to return errors. Scammers often ask for wires because they are fast and hard to reverse.
feedback: Wires are fast and generally final, which is why scammers prefer them.

misconceptions.B: A stop payment may be possible

correct_answer: A fake-check scam
question: A buyer sends Liam a cashier's check for $1,500 for a $500 phone and asks him to wire back the extra $1,000. What is most likely happening?
intro: A cashier's check is drawn on the bank's own funds, so a real one is very reliable. But fake cashier's checks are common. The bank may make the money available before discovering the check is fake; when it bounces, you owe the bank the full amount.
feedback: Overpayment with a request to send money back is a classic fake-check scam. Liam would owe the bank when the check bounces.

misconceptions.B: Ignores the classic overpayment scam pattern
misconceptions.D: Thinks the bank absorbs fraud losses

correct_answer: An employer's direct deposit of paychecks
question: Which is a typical use of an ACH transfer?
intro: The ACH (Automated Clearing House) network moves money electronically between bank accounts in batches. It is cheaper and slower than a wire transfer.
feedback: Direct deposit and many automatic bill payments use the ACH network.

correct_answer: Call a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions
question: Before wiring money for a home or apartment deposit, what is the safest step?
intro: Criminals hack or fake emails and send new "updated" wire instructions so money goes to their account. Because wires are hard to reverse, verify instructions through a trusted phone number, not one in the suspicious email.
feedback: Independent verification defeats changed-instructions scams.

misconceptions.C: Uses the same possibly hacked channel

correct_answer: A stop payment order through her bank
question: Ruth wrote a check and then learned it was lost in the mail before it was cashed. What service could stop it?
intro: Until a check is paid by your bank, you can ask the bank not to pay it. Banks usually charge a fee for this service, and it does not work on a check that has already cleared.
feedback: A stop payment order tells the bank not to pay that check, if it has not already cleared.

correct_answer: Check her own account directly and send nothing
question: Someone texts Ava: "I sent you $200 by mistake — please send it back!" Her app shows no new money in her account. What should she do?
intro: A common scam claims you received money "by mistake" and asks you to send it back. Sometimes the original payment was made with stolen information and is later reversed, leaving you with the loss. Verify inside your own app or bank, never through a link or message.
feedback: Without verified money in her own account, there is nothing to return. Even if money did arrive, contact the app's support rather than sending money.

misconceptions.D: Still sends money to a scammer

correct_answer: Multi-factor authentication and a passcode on the app
question: Which setting adds the most protection to a payment app?
feedback: Multi-factor authentication and an app passcode make unauthorized access much harder.

correct_answer: An imposter scam
question: A "customer support" caller says your payment app is hacked and asks you to send your balance to a "safe account." What is this?
intro: Real banks and payment apps do not ask you to move money to a "safe account" to protect it. Imposters pretend to be bank staff, tech support, or government officials and create urgency.
feedback: Any request to move money to protect it is a red flag for an imposter scam. Hang up and call the official number.

misconceptions.A: Real companies do not ask this
misconceptions.C: Believes real support asks for codes

correct_answer: A transfer someone else made from your account without permission
question: Which payment is generally protected under federal error rules (Regulation E)?
feedback: Regulation E protections focus on unauthorized transfers and certain errors; payments you authorize, even to scammers, are often not covered.

correct_answer: Confirming who the recipient is through a source you trust
question: Before sending money with a payment app to someone new, which step lowers the risk the MOST?
feedback: Verifying who you are paying, through a channel you trust, prevents most P2P losses.

question: Jada earns $16.50 per hour and works 24 hours this week. What is her gross pay for the week?
intro: An hourly wage is the amount paid for each hour of work. Gross pay is the total earned before taxes or any other deductions are taken out. For hourly work: gross pay = hourly wage × hours worked.

misconceptions.A: Adds the wage and the hours

question: Malik is an hourly employee who earns $18 per hour. He works 46 hours in one workweek. Under the federal overtime rule, what is his gross pay?
intro: Federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act) requires most hourly employees to be paid at least 1.5 times their regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a workweek. This is "time and a half." Hours up to 40 are paid at the regular rate.
feedback: Regular: 40 × $18 = $720. Overtime rate: $18 × 1.5 = $27. Overtime: 6 × $27 = $162. Total: $882.

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at the overtime rate

correct_answer: His total earnings before any deductions
question: Malik's pay stub shows "Gross pay: $882." What does gross pay mean?
intro: Paychecks show two key amounts. Gross pay is everything earned for the period. Net pay ("take-home pay") is what is left after deductions such as taxes and benefit costs, and it is what is actually deposited.
feedback: Gross pay is the total earned before deductions; net pay is what he takes home.

misconceptions.B: Confuses gross pay with net pay
misconceptions.C: Thinks gross pay is partly after deductions

question: Ana's timecard shows Monday 6.5 hours, Wednesday 4.25 hours, and Saturday 8 hours. She earns $15.20 per hour. What is her gross pay?
intro: Timecards often record hours in decimals: 15 minutes is 0.25 hour, 30 minutes is 0.5 hour, and 45 minutes is 0.75 hour. Add the hours first, then multiply by the hourly wage.

misconceptions.B: Drops the quarter hour and uses 18 hours

correct_answer: Job A, by $17.50
question: Two summer jobs require 30 hours a week. Job A pays $17.25 per hour. Job B pays a flat $500 per week. Which pays more per week, and by how much?

misconceptions.C: Uses one hour's wage as the difference
misconceptions.D: Does not compute the hourly total

correct_answer: The worker earns $14 for each hour worked
question: A job pays $14 per hour. What does that mean?
intro: A wage is a rate: dollars per hour. The more hours you work, the more you earn.
feedback: $14 per hour means $14 for every hour worked.

misconceptions.A: Confuses a wage with a daily amount
misconceptions.B: Confuses a wage with a weekly salary

question: Rina earns $14 per hour and works 10 hours. How much does she earn?
intro: Earnings for hourly work = wage × hours.

correct_answer: 7.25 hours
question: How many hours is 7 hours and 15 minutes, written as a decimal?
intro: An hour has 60 minutes. To change minutes to part of an hour, divide by 60: 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25.
feedback: 15 minutes = 15/60 = 0.25 hour, so 7 h 15 min = 7.25 hours.

misconceptions.A: Writes minutes as hundredths of an hour
misconceptions.B: Treats 15 minutes as half an hour

correct_answer: Gross pay
question: Which number on a paycheck shows earnings BEFORE taxes are taken out?
intro: "Gross" pay is the full amount earned. "Net" pay, also called take-home pay, is what remains after deductions.
feedback: Gross pay is before deductions.

question: Leo's wage rises from $15 to $16 per hour. He works 20 hours a week. How much more does he earn each week?
intro: A raise in the hourly wage adds that amount for every hour worked.
feedback: $1 more per hour × 20 hours = $20 more per week.

misconceptions.A: Gives the raise per hour, not per week

correct_answer: 0 hours
question: Jon works 10 hours a day, Monday through Thursday, and no other hours that week. Under the federal rule, how many overtime hours does he earn?
intro: Federal overtime is based on hours in a WORKWEEK (any fixed, repeating 7-day period), not hours in a day. A few states also require daily overtime, so state law can add protection.
feedback: 4 × 10 = 40 hours, which is not over 40 in the workweek, so there is no federal overtime. A state with daily overtime rules could require more.

misconceptions.C: Counts one whole day as overtime

correct_answer: No overtime pay is required
question: A salaried store manager meets the legal tests for an "exempt" employee and works 50 hours one week. What overtime pay does federal law require?
intro: Some salaried employees are "exempt" from overtime because they are paid at least a minimum salary and their main duties are executive, administrative, or professional. Being paid a salary alone does not make someone exempt; the duties test also matters.
feedback: Exempt employees are not entitled to overtime pay under federal law, even for long weeks.

question: Pia earns $20 per hour and works 52 hours in a workweek. What is her gross pay?

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at time and a half

correct_answer: No; it depends on employer policy
question: Does federal law require employers to pay time and a half for working on a holiday, when the week totals 32 hours?
intro: The federal overtime law does not require extra pay for holidays or weekends. Many employers offer holiday pay as a policy, and union contracts may require it, but that is not the federal rule.
feedback: Holiday premium pay comes from employer policy or contracts, not the FLSA; at 32 hours, no overtime applies.

question: Job A pays $19 per hour and usually schedules 45 hours a week (overtime applies). How much does Job A pay for a typical week?

misconceptions.A: Pays every hour at the regular rate
misconceptions.C: Pays the overtime hours at double time
misconceptions.D: Pays every hour at time and a half

question: Kai, a server, worked 25 hours at a cash wage of $5.00 per hour and earned $410 in tips. What were his total earnings for the week?
intro: In many restaurant jobs, pay has two parts: an hourly cash wage from the employer and tips from customers. Some states allow a lower cash wage for tipped workers (a "tip credit"), and others require the full minimum wage before tips.

misconceptions.C: Adds hours instead of wage × hours

question: Kai earned $535 in wages and tips for 25 hours of work. What were his average earnings per hour?

correct_answer: He reports them to his employer; they are taxable
question: Kai received $410 in tips this month. What does the IRS require?
intro: Tips are taxable income. Employees who receive $20 or more in tips in a month must report them to their employer, who includes them in payroll records and withholding.
feedback: Monthly tips of $20 or more must be reported to the employer, and tips are taxable.

question: In a state where the minimum wage is $15.00 per hour and a tip credit is allowed, Lia works 20 hours at a $5.00 cash wage and earns $150 in tips. Federal rules require her total to reach at least minimum wage for those hours. How much must her employer add?
intro: When an employer pays a lower cash wage and counts tips toward the minimum wage, the employer must make up the difference if wages plus tips fall below the full minimum wage for the hours worked.
feedback: Required: 20 × $15 = $300. She received $100 + $150 = $250. The employer must add $50.

misconceptions.C: Gives her tips as the amount owed

correct_answer: Plan around a lower weekly amount and save the extra
question: Kai's tips vary from $250 to $500 a week. Which budgeting approach is safest?
feedback: With uneven income, budgeting on a conservative amount and saving surpluses smooths slow weeks.

misconceptions.C: Leaves no cushion for slow weeks

question: A full-time job pays a salary of $41,600 per year. Full-time is 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). What is the equivalent hourly rate?
intro: A salary is a fixed yearly amount, often paid in equal paychecks. To compare a salary with an hourly wage, use the number of hours worked in a year. A common full-time estimate is 40 hours × 52 weeks = 2,080 hours.

question: Ryan earns $41,600 a year, paid biweekly (every two weeks). What is his gross pay per paycheck?
intro: Pay frequency affects each paycheck's size: weekly = 52 paychecks per year; biweekly (every two weeks) = 26; semimonthly (twice a month, such as the 1st and 15th) = 24; monthly = 12.
feedback: $41,600 ÷ 26 = $1,600.00 per biweekly paycheck.

question: Erin earns $41,600 a year, paid semimonthly (twice a month, 24 paychecks a year). What is her gross pay per paycheck (to the nearest cent)?
feedback: Semimonthly means 24 paychecks: $41,600 ÷ 24 = $1,733.33.

question: Dev earns $22 per hour and works 40 hours a week for 52 weeks. What is his yearly gross pay?

correct_answer: Biweekly (every two weeks)
question: Which pay schedule gives a worker three paychecks in two months of most years?
intro: A year has 12 months but 52 weeks. Schedules based on weeks do not line up evenly with months, while schedules based on dates in the month always do.
feedback: Biweekly pay gives 26 paychecks a year, so two months have three paychecks. Semimonthly is always two per month.

question: How many weeks are in a year?
intro: A year has 52 weeks (and a day or two more). Since 52 ÷ 12 ≈ 4.33, a month is about 4.33 weeks, not exactly 4.
feedback: A year has 52 weeks.

correct_answer: About $2,167
question: Tom earns $500 a week. Which is the best estimate of his MONTHLY pay?
intro: To turn weekly pay into monthly pay accurately, find yearly pay first (× 52), then divide by 12.

question: A job pays $2,400 per month. What is the yearly pay?
intro: To turn monthly pay into yearly pay, multiply by 12.

correct_answer: A set yearly amount, paid in paychecks
question: What is a "salary"?
intro: Hourly workers are paid for each hour worked. Salaried workers are paid a set amount per year, usually split evenly across paychecks, regardless of small changes in hours.
feedback: A salary is a set annual amount paid in regular paychecks.

question: How many hours does a full-time worker at 40 hours a week work in 52 weeks?

correct_answer: Offer B, by $1,000
question: Offer A: $21 per hour, 40 hours a week, 50 paid weeks a year. Offer B: salary of $43,000. Which pays more per year, and by how much?
intro: To compare offers, put them on the same basis, usually yearly gross pay. Count only weeks that are actually paid.

question: Offer C pays $19 per hour, but expected overtime adds 5 hours at time and a half every week for 50 weeks. What is the yearly pay from the overtime alone?
